title: Let the importer bind records

blocks.text: The nightly import reads CSV rows into DTOs through `RowBinder`, which was written when every DTO was a JavaBean. This sprint the team turned the DTOs into records, and the first import after the release failed on its first row with `NoSuchMethodException: ...<init>()`.

`RowBinder.bind` already sends records to `bindRecord`. Finish the `TODO` in `src/main/java/practice/RowBinder.java` so that `bindRecord` builds the record from the row. The row is a map from column name to value, as the CSV reader produced it: numbers arrive boxed, and the columns come in the file's order, which is not always the order of the record's components. When a record refuses a value, the import reports the record's own exception, the one its author wrote the message for.

cases.says: a row with one column per component binds to the record with those values
a record bound from a row has gone through its own constructor, so its normalisation applies
each component takes the column with its own name, whatever order the row's columns come in
a component of a primitive type binds from a row that holds the boxed value
when the record's constructor refuses a value, the caller gets the exception the record threw

origin.section: A Binder Can Build a Record Only Through Its Canonical Constructor

concepts: A record has no no-arg constructor and its fields can't be written by reflection, so a binder must pass the values, matched by component name and type, to the canonical constructor, which runs the record's own checks.
